title: Why Struggle with Continuous Latents? Interpretable Discrete Latent Reasoning via Rendered Compression
claim: Continuous latent reasoning lacks discrete anchors and is hard to inspect; discrete latent tokens anchor reasoning and fix this.
layout: Top supervision banner above 2 side-by-side panels (a)/(b); warning icons vs codebook
description: A top orange banner shows a math word problem with Question, Explicit CoT (dashed grey box) and Answer. Below are two rounded panels. Panel (a), blue, shows Continuous Latent Reasoning: Question tokens go into an LLM, then a dashed region of wobbly circled hidden states h1, h2, h3 to hn, then Output tokens. Yellow warning icons mark the problems: lacking explicit discrete anchors (dashed boxes with red crosses), reasoning process hard to inspect, and errors can accumulate across steps. Panel (b), purple, shows Discrete Latent Reasoning: the CoT is rendered as a handwritten-style image and fed to a Latent Codebook. The LLM then emits discrete tokens <id_1>…<id_5> before the Answer and Output, with cross-entropy loss cycles. Orange question and answer tokens and blue output tokens carry through both panels. The eye goes first to the banner and then to the contrasting panels.
caption: Continuous latent reasoning suffers from a mismatch between its intermediate states and discrete symbolic supervision, resulting in a training bottleneck, unstable reasoning dynamics, and poor interpretability. Our approach resolves this by introducing discrete latent tokens as anchors within the reasoning process, enabling standard autoregressive training and controllable latent reasoning.
abstract: Large language models achieve high reasoning performance via explicit chain-of-thought and reinforcement learning, but require long output sequences and extended inference time. Latent reasoning reduces this cost by shifting computation into a latent space; however, continuous latent methods are hard to train, suffering from unstable and uninterpretable reasoning trajectories. We argue these issues stem from a misalignment between continuous-space reasoning and discrete symbolic supervision, as continuous states lack explicit anchors for step-by-step alignment. To resolve this, we propose \textbf{Discrete Latent Reasoning~(DLR)}, the first method that converts continuous latent states into explicit discrete tokens. Inspired by render-based compression, we render textual chains of thought into images, extract visual features, and construct a discrete latent vocabulary via clustering-based fine-tuning. Expanding the vocabulary and output head enables standard autoregressive modeling over both natural language and latent tokens, supporting pretraining alignment, SFT, and RL. Experiments on five reasoning benchmarks and two model series~(Qwen3-VL and LLaMA-3) confirm that \textbf{DLR} outperforms prior latent reasoning baselines with up to \textbf{20$\times$ compression}. Furthermore, the learned latent trajectories retain an interpretable semantic structure. Overall, discrete latent tokens provide a controllable and interpretable basis for efficient latent reasoning. Code is available at github.com/Miraclecsc/Discrete-Latent-Reasoning
